title: 55 Years, 55 Tracks: How the Labèque Sisters Keep Reinventing the Piano Duo
summary: In 1969, at the Paris Conservatoire, two headstrong sisters made a choice that would define their lives. Katia and Marielle Labèque were rehearsing Olivier Messiaen's thorny Visions de l'Amen when the legendary composer himself walked in. Impressed, he offered to record the piece with one of them and his wife. The sisters refused. They were a duo, and they were staying that way. Messiaen backed down and supervised their first recording—a movement of which now closes their new triple album, 55. The album is a toast to over 55 years of recording, but it's no mere greatest-hits collection. Nearly half of its 55 tracks are brand new, and they carry a deliberate message. The Labèques are spotlighting women composers they admit they've neglected. There's sturdy, angular music by Polish composer Grażyna Bacewicz, finally getting her due, and a haunting piece by Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou, the enigmatic Ethiopian nun who died in 2023. Lili Boulanger, the gifted sister of famed pedagogue Nadia Boulanger, appears alongside a powerful arrangement of Margaret Bonds's "Troubled Water." The set careens between ferocious two-piano duets and delicate four-handed works. Stravinsky's Rite of Spring, in a two-piano arrangement, sounds like a feral beast clawing out of the instruments. Then there's Marie Jaëll's little waltz, Op. 8, No. 8—a beguiling mix of dark shadows and French charm from a composer who was friends with Liszt and, in 1893, became the first French pianist to perform all 32 Beethoven sonatas. The sisters also step apart for a few solo moments: Katia joins Chick Corea for a tender "We Will Meet Again," while Marielle interprets Erik Satie and Bryce Dessner of The National. What Messiaen heard in 1969 remains their calling card: extraordinary precision, a telepathic ability to finish each other's musical sentences, warmth of tone, and a palpable fearlessness. For over half a century, Katia and Marielle Labèque have redefined what two pianists can sound like—and this album proves they're still pushing boundaries.
why_it_matters: For young people, the Labèque sisters' story demonstrates that refusing to compromise your identity can lead to a career that redefines a whole art form. It also shows how today's artists can reshape history by bringing forgotten voices back into the spotlight.

background_read: The Paris Conservatoire is one of the world's most historic music schools, and it was there that the sisters met Olivier Messiaen (1908–1992), a French composer famous for using birdsong and complex rhythms.
The Labèques, born in Bayonne, France, rose to fame in the 1980s with their energetic Gershwin duet and have since worked with artists from rock to jazz, blending genres.

The album's spotlight on women composers reflects a wider effort to correct past neglect: Grażyna Bacewicz (a Polish violinist-composer), Emahoy Tsegué-Maryam Guèbrou (an Ethiopian nun who fused classical and Ethiopian music), Lili Boulanger (the first woman to win the Prix de Rome in 1913), and Margaret Bonds (an African American composer and Langston Hughes collaborator) are finally receiving attention.

The sisters' recording also includes solo moments with Chick Corea (a pioneering jazz pianist) and pieces by contemporary composer Bryce Dessner of The National, showing how the piano duo remains a site of constant reinvention.

perspectives.description: The album celebrates women composers and revives unjustly neglected music, expanding the classical canon. The sisters' decades-long partnership proves the power of artistic loyalty and refusing to split up, showing that staying true to each other can change an entire genre.

Some might argue that the album's mix of styles feels disjointed, or that spotlighting women composers now could be seen as performative after decades of neglect. The duo's earlier neglect of these composers also raises questions about why recognition came so late.

Historically, piano duos were once common but declined; the Labèques revived the format, blending classical with contemporary genres. The album's structure mirrors the fragmented way music is consumed today, while their career shows how a duo can adapt across eras.

The album may inspire a new generation of duo pianists and lead to more inclusive programming in concert halls. It could encourage broader audience engagement with overlooked composers and push record labels to fund more exploratory, multi-composer projects.
